items.title: Crashing Microcontrollers Competitively
items.summary: [Ani] has produced rather an interesting game. Kacken Open Air (KOA) is a browser-based game, wherein players compete for access to a limited resource—namely, festival toilets. So far, so amusing, but there’s a neat technical twist. You’re actually competing to crash microcontrollers in the real world (German, Google Translate link ). The way the game works is simple enough. There are more players than there are toilets, so players have to fight over them. This is achieved by knocking on the toilet doors in the game. However, paired to each toilet in the game is a real ESP8266 microcontroller. Each knock from a player adds computational load to the microcontroller. Knock enough, and the microcontroller will slow enough, and the player occupying the toilet will be kicked out. Keep knocking, and eventually the microcontroller will run out of memory, crash, and reboot. In game, this causes the toilet to collapse. The whole setup runs on a cluster of microcontrollers, with an ESP32-P4, a bunch of ESP8266s, a few Raspberry Pi Pico 2s, Arduino Dues, and an STM8 working as a hardware watchdog to make sure everything stays alive when it should. If you want to sample the game, try it out in your browser here. (German, Google Translate link ). It’s a really fun concept to combine hardware performance with actual gameplay outcomes. It’s so totally different from other projects we’ve seen that involve gaming on ESP microcontrollers. If you’ve done something similar, or something totally zany and different, bell us on the tipsline either way! Please be kind and respectful to help make the comments section excellent. items.title: DabbleCAD Takes Design Offline
items.summary: These days, there are all kind of online-only and in-browser CAD packages. DabbleCAD is the opposite of all that— a simple, offline, open-source design solution. DabbleCAD handles 3D design in a similar way to TinkerCAD. It’s shape based modelling, with all the usual tools for stretching, deforming, punching holes, and the like. It’s set up to export your geometry to STL or 3MF so you can throw it straight into a slicer for 3D printing. However, it’s also a package that can handle design for laser cutters, too. There are simple tools for importing artwork or drawing it from scratch, and it will export the relevant G-code or directly send to a GRBL-compatible laser cutter hooked up over USB. As a nice bonus, there’s also an engraving feature. 3D models or images can be turned into height maps for relief engraving if you’ve got the tools for it. DabbleCAD doesn’t do anything groundbreaking or new that existing software can’t handle. It’s just a convenient, portable piece of software in an era when so much of what we use is tied to logins and clouds and endless headaches around connectivity . items.title: Preventing a Garage Door Opener From Rebooting When Offline
items.summary: It’s always great when a smart garage door opener allows for easy local integration into a smart home network, but it’s not so nice when said device still insists on connecting to certain remote servers, and even reboots constantly due to time-outs. This was the problem that [Kusha] was facing with a LiftMaster MyQ Home Bridge garage door control. The solution ended up being to dump the key for the encrypted MQTT communication and setting up a dummy server. The encryption key is stored on the Cortex-M4 MCU, with fortunately the debug interface with the SWD pins and everything else left in plain view on the PCB. From there it only takes a bit of creative wiring and a bit of Arduino code to read out the needed data. After this you still need to set up an MQTT broker with this key installed and capable of serving pings to the device after it connects. For this part [Kusha] provides a Docker configuration to streamline this process if you are into containers. Setting up an existing Mosquito or similar MQTT broker for secure MQTT access isn’t overly complicated otherwise. Of course the device will still try to connect to the mqdevice.com domains where the manufacturer’s MQTT brokers are running, but with a local DNS server you can gently coax these to be redirected to your own MQTT broker instead. After this the device will be convinced that it’s now Cloud-Enabled and stop trying to reboot all the time to fix the egregious problem of not having internet access after being put on an IoT VLAN or similar. Cut your losses, get out of the toxic relationship and actually solve the problem without ‘doing too much’. Reset/disconnect it from any HomeKit services like it’s just a regular opener, and wire in a simple HomeKit compatible button presser + door state sensor like a Meross.

items.title: A Big Ol’ LED Matrix Cube
items.summary: You could have a featureless cube in your house, but that would be boring, and we wouldn’t write a Hackaday article about it. Alternatively, you could whip up a cube that is positively covered in LEDs that play all sorts of animations, like [Ross Harvey] did. The cube that [Ross] built has six faces covered in HUB75 LED panels, each consisting of 64 x 64 LEDs in a 2.5 mm pitch measuring 160 mm square. That’s a total of 24,576 individually addressable LEDs, if you’re counting along at home. Each face has a cell-cast acrylic diffuser sheet, which gives the LEDs a much smoother, more pleasant appearance when lit. Inside the cube lives a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 paired with a custom HUB75 driver board, as well as a power/boost board that draws from a 2-cell lithium-ion pack. There are also two speakers and a microphone hooked up, which provides for both audio feedback and audio reactivity. The cube can display all kinds of things, from various games to music visualizers and even a rather tasteful world clock setup. You can build the cube yourself if you really want six sides of glowing glory on your desk. However, if you’re strapped for time, [Ross] later developed an off-the-shelf version for all your cubey needs. If you prefer more complicated solids, it’s hard to go past [Greg Davill’s] classic glowing D20 build. Video after the break. items.title: Digital Badge Gets Reverse Engineered
items.summary: The JieLi AC707N is a cheap $10 digital badge that actually packs in a fair bit of interesting hardware. [Sabas] reverse-engineered the product and figured out how to flash custom firmware onto sealed OEM-fresh units. The AC707N badge, of the BR35 family, comes well equipped out of the box. It has a 360×360 pixel round display, driven over QSPI. It comes equipped with a AXS5106L capacitive touch controller for interacting with the screen. There are also two buttons, 4MB of flash, and Bluetooth Low Energy capability on board. Plenty to play with, right there! [Sabas] gave a talk about how the device was first physically torn down, before the APK was decompiled in Ghidra. From there, it was possible to download the firmware without authentication and then develop an open SDK for working with the cheap device. There’s a custom firmware available on Github that was developed a a result of these efforts, and it can do all kinds of neat things. You can use it as a Bluetooth Mouse, or a Bluetooth scanner, for example. Or, if so desired, you could build on this work and develop your own firmware for the device to suit your own use cases. We see stuff like this repurposed all the time. The GeekMagic SmallTV is a great example of a cheap device given greater functionality through custom firmware . Video after the break. Very cool! items.title: Monitors that Throttle Downloads
items.summary: Displays in general are a lot more complicated now than they used to be, but even still, you’d be forgiven for not expecting a monitor to slow down your internet connection. Yet that’s exactly what [Oscar] ran into recently , and fortunately for us, he was good enough to document how he figured out what was going on. This bug might not have been discovered at all except for the fact that [Oscar] enjoys a 2.5 Gbps symmetric internet connection. When running a speed test he found he was getting the advertised speed for upload, but download was somehow limited to 600 Mbps. This was only with the USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter he uses plugged into the monitor , which is acting as a hub. When it was plugged directly into the computer there were no dropped packets and he was able to get full speed. But the curious thing was the operating system was not noticing the dropped packets, so something was going on before the monitor was getting involved. A driver update brought the speed to around 1.1 Gbps which was an improvement, but there was still a problem. Then [Oscar] tried using Ethernet flow control, which asks the sender of the packets to pause briefly if the receiver is dropping frames, rather than losing those frames completely. This also improved things, but still not completely. And it had the feeling of a workaround as well. What he’s settled on having been the problem in a nutshell is that the buffer on the 2.5 Gbps card would fill before the data would transfer through the hub to the computer, and if it overflows it will drop packets. The solution was to upgrade to a 5 Gbps card with a larger buffer, and after that there were no more dropped frames. We might consider upgrading to fiber for faster speeds though. items.title: How Apple’s HomeView Actively Resists Repairs
items.summary: Over the past years there have been hopeful noises about Apple devices becoming easier to service and repair, but as [iFixit] found with their teardown of the new HomeView devices , such optimism may be premature. In this teardown they found that extremely strong adhesive is used for the display, as well as to keep the speakers in place. Even worse is that the mainboard’s back metal can is effectively glued in place with thermal compound, and the speaker connectors on the mainboard pretty much disintegrate if you try to unplug them, even after trying to scrape off the glue on them. All of this leads to a pretty miserable teardown experience, with the display removal probably being the easiest part. Even plentiful IPA application and careful prying cannot save one of the big speaker modules, with both their connectors mauled as well. The rear metal can of the mainboard is left in place, probably requiring liberal dousing in IPA or stronger solvents to loosen up first, as well as borderline inaccessible screws, and the subwoofer in the base is basically impossible to plug back into place after disassembly. Looking at the wall-mounted version of the HomeView , things do not get much better, but it omits the subwoofer and screw issues of the base version. Overall this seems like the kind of device that’s somewhat repairable if you go in armed with all this knowledge that [iFixit] sacrificed a HomeView for, but it’s disappointing to see such a repair nightmare in 2026. Interestingly, this device is not available in the EU, purportedly due to the privacy nightmare that is the Siri AI feature, but it may run afoul of some right-to-repair regulations too, or at the very least get assigned a very low score. items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases
